title: Two monks and a river
hookLine: Tanzan carries a woman across a stream, and hours later Ekido is still carrying her in his head (Zen story, Japan)
carry: I set her down at the river

cards: Two in the morning. Someone lies awake replaying a remark from lunch. Or from last week.
Or from years ago. The person who said it has long forgotten it, and is fast asleep. And the remark is still being turned over, carried around the dark room.
Now, two monks walking home in the rain, Tanzan and Ekido. The water is high and the road is a mess, and at the crossing stands a young woman in a silk kimono who can't get across.
Tanzan does something his companion will not stop thinking about for hours.

teach.b: Tanzan doesn't hesitate. Come on, he says. He picks her up, carries her across the water, sets her down on the other side, and walks on.
Ekido says nothing, all afternoon, all the way to the temple. But he's boiling. These monks had vowed to keep their distance from women, and his companion just picked one up in the road.
That night he can't hold it in. We monks aren't supposed to go near women, he says. Especially not young and lovely ones.
Why did you do that? And Tanzan answers: I set her down at the river.
Are you still carrying her? A word on the details: in the twentieth-century English telling, the crossing is a flooded, muddy road; later retellings made it a river, and the river stuck.
Tanzan is remembered as a real Zen teacher with a habit of breaking conventions. Now look who's really carrying the woman. Tanzan held her for a minute, to help, and let her go.
Ekido never touched her, and he carried her for hours in his head, heavier with every step.

teach.h: THE WEIGHT IS IN THE HOLDING ON.
teach.b: The weight wasn't in the act. It was in the holding on. The old insult.
The awkward moment. The thing you should have said. The thing that was done, and finished, long ago.

teach.h: I SET HER DOWN AT THE RIVER.
teach.b: Zen teachers have a word for letting go: hōge, casting down.

how: Zen teachers tell the story of Tanzan and Ekido when talking about letting go, and in meditation practice people notice a thought they keep returning to and set it down, again and again.

o: letting go, setting down what you hold
a pilgrim's crossing of a flooded river
a monk's vow to keep apart from others

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: carried her across and walked on
carried her in his head all day
couldn't get across in her kimono

he said nothing all afternoon, and only burst out that night at the temple.

with a habit of breaking conventions.

games.q: you're Tanzan, a monk who has vowed to keep his distance from women. a young woman can't get across the flooded crossing. what do you do?
o: walk past; your vows come first.
pick her up, carry her across, and walk on.
wait with her until the water goes down.
games.why: he carries her over and sets her down. hours later Ekido is still upset, and Tanzan asks: I set her down at the river. are you still carrying her?

practice: Find something that happened, and is over, but that you're still holding, a remark, a mistake, an argument that ended days ago, and feel where you carry it: shoulders, jaw, stomach.
Then picture a river, walk to the far bank, and set it down on the ground there. You don't have to forget it; just stop carrying it for now.

wordCard.voice: Hōge, the Zen word for letting go, casting down. Tanzan sets the woman down at the river; Ekido carries her in his head all day.

orig.note: Japanese, hōge: letting go, casting down, a Zen word for dropping what you're holding.

carryVoice: Your line: I set her down at the river. Ekido never even touched her. See you tomorrow.
